1. The product and the person

The user: a home-based food or craft seller (a cake baker, a short-eats caterer, a handmade jewelry maker) who takes 10–40 orders a day over WhatsApp. Customers write in Sinhala, English, or romanized Sinhala (“Singlish”) in the same chat, often in one sentence: “ada ratta 1kg chocolate cake ekak, Sunday evening ekata, Peradeniya”.

The problem today: every evening she scrolls through dozens of chats, copies orders into a notebook or spreadsheet, and works out what to bake or make and where to deliver. Orders get missed, a changed date gets overlooked, and a cancelled order still gets baked. That’s 45–90 minutes a day, and a single mistake costs a 1 kg cake and a customer’s trust.

Why she’d pay: the tool gives back an hour a day and prevents the occasional costly error. One avoided wrong order pays for months of the subscription.

2. The open-source stack
Component	Role	Why it’s load-bearing
Qwen3-8B (Apache 2.0), 4-bit quantized	Reads a customer thread and extracts the order	Multilingual enough to handle Sinhala/English mixing, and its weights can be fine-tuned on one seller’s chats
Ollama / llama.cpp	Local inference runtime	Runs on a 16 GB laptop with no internet and exposes JSON-schema-constrained output, so the model can only return valid order records
SQLite + Python (FastAPI)	Local ledger and review UI	Orders, catalog, and corrections never leave the machine
openpyxl	Exports the day’s sheets	Produces the production list and delivery list as Excel files she can already use

The structured-output feature matters most. The model fills a fixed schema instead of writing free text, which removes the largest source of garbage in extraction.

3. Why open matters here

Four reasons actually apply to this product:

Customer data is other people’s data. Chats contain names, phone numbers, and home addresses. “Your customers’ chats ne
<truncated 2914 bytes>
n, and build a 50-chat test set from her corrections.

Pricing test (three arms across the first 10 sellers):

A one-time license around LKR 8,000–10,000
A monthly plan around LKR 2,000–2,500
A free trial that converts to the monthly plan after 14 days

These are starting guesses to be tested, not conclusions. The key signal is whether she pre-pays or commits to a date, not whether she says it’s useful.

What I measure:

Field accuracy without edits (target ≥ 90% on date, quantity, product)
Minutes saved per evening, self-reported and timed
Missed or wrong orders before versus after
Daily use in week 2, as the best retention proxy
Conversion at each price point

If sellers love it but won’t pay at any tested price, the idea fails, and that’s a useful result.

6. Honest limits
Quality gap on Sinhala and Singlish. An 8B model will misread messy messages that a frontier model gets right. Handling: the review screen plus confidence flags make errors cheap to catch, and corrections improve it per seller.
Hardware. An 8B model at 4-bit needs about 16 GB of RAM and runs slowly on CPU. Handling: run extraction as a batch (“process today’s chats”) rather than live, and stay within her hardware.
Installation and support. A local tool is harder to install than a website. Handling: a one-click installer later, and hands-on setup for the first customers.
Evaluation risk. I can’t trust a model on Sinhala without measuring it. Handling: the 50-chat test set on day one, and a model swap if Qwen3 loses on it.
Voice notes are out of scope. Many orders arrive as voice messages, which this version doesn’t handle.

   - Automatically detects **Ollama (Qwen3-8B / Qwen2.5)** when available.
